name: Denis Pelli
title: Professor of Psychology and Neural Science
bio: Denis G. Pelli is a Professor of Psychology and Neural Science at NYU since 1995, focusing on object recognition and the experience of beauty. His educational background includes a BA in applied mathematics from Harvard University and a PhD in Physiology from Cambridge University. He completed postdoctoral work on psychophysics of reading under Gordon Legge at the University of Minnesota. Notable honors include the 2000 Optical Society of America Leadership Award/New Focus Prize, recognizing his contributions to visual science benefiting artists, scholars and the visually impaired. He served as a Visiting Fellow Commoner at Trinity College, Cambridge (2011-2012) and received the 2016 Oberdorfer Low Vision Award from ARVO. His scholarship has generated approximately 20,000 citations according to Google Scholar.

name: G. Bard Ermentrout
roundtables: What Can Mathematics Teach Us About Mind/Brain?

name: Josefa Ros Velasco
title: Associate in the Department of Romance Languages and Literatures; Real Colegio Complutense at Harvard Postdoctoral Fellow
bio: Dr. Ros Velasco conducts multidisciplinary research on the evolutionary role of boredom from a philosophical-anthropological point of view to challenge the understanding of boredom as pathological. She examines how boredom became medicalized through nineteenth-century literature and philosophy. Her published works include three edited/authored books: Feminism. Past, Present, and Future Perspectives (2017), Contemporary Approaches in Philosophical and Humanistic Thought (2017), and Hans Blumenberg. Literatura, estetica y nihilismo (2016). Academic papers include works on Blumenberg's philosophical anthropology of boredom, humanizing treatment approaches, and comprehensive boredom studies (2017-2018). She is developing a forthcoming book on boredom's pathologization history and plans future research on boredom in aging populations to improve seniors' quality of life.

name: Tal Rabin
title: Research Staff Member and Manager of Cryptographic Research Group
bio: Tal Rabin manages the Cryptography Research Group at IBM's T.J. Watson Research Center, focusing on cryptography and, more specifically, on secure multiparty computation, threshold cryptography and proactive security. She earned her Ph.D. in Computer Science from Hebrew University, Israel (1994) and completed an NSF Postdoc Fellowship at MIT (1994-1996) before joining IBM Research in 1996. She has held leadership roles including Program and General Chair positions at major cryptography conferences and serves as an editor of the Journal of Cryptology. Her professional service includes membership on the SIGACT Executive Board, Computing Community Consortium council, and the Association of Women in Mathematics membership committee. She founded and organizes the Women in Theory Workshop, a biennial graduate student event. Rabin has received media coverage in the New York Times, World Science Festival, and WNYC's Science Fair.

name: Tyler Volk
title: Professor of Biology and Environmental Studies
bio: Tyler Volk is a professor at NYU exploring complexity across scales. His 2017 work "Quarks to Culture: How We Came to Be" examines what he terms "combogenesis" -- the mechanism creating organizational levels from elementary particles through human civilization. He proposes that physics and chemistry generated biological evolution, which in turn produced cultural evolution. Prior publications include "CO2 Rising: The World's Greatest Environmental Challenge" (2008), "Gaia's Body: Toward a Physiology of Earth" (1998), and "Metapatterns Across Space, Time, and Mind" (1995). He has received NYU's Distinguished Teaching Award and Golden Dozen Award.
roundtables: Complexity and Emergence II: Visions of Cosmic Order, from Particles to People

name: Danielle Reed
title: Chief Science Officer
bio: Danielle Renee Reed is the Chief Science Officer of the Monell Chemical Senses Center, a non-profit research institution devoted to the study of taste and smell, located in Philadelphia. She received her Ph.D. in Psychology from Yale University, and did her postdoctoral training in genetics at the University of Pennsylvania. She studies person-to-person differences in the sense of taste and smell, is the past president of the Association of Chemoreception Sciences and a founding member of the Global Consortium for Chemosensory Research, and was recently awarded a patent for smell screening test. Currently she is working on a collaborative grant to understand the molecular basis of post-viral taste and smell loss.

name: Jennifer Ratner-Rosenhagen
title: Merle Curti and Vilas Borghesi Distinguished Achievement Professor of History
bio: Jennifer Ratner-Rosenhagen is a historian whose scholarly work concentrates on the intellectual and cultural history of the United States in transatlantic perspective. She authored three major works: American Nietzsche (2012), The Ideas that Made America (2019), and American Intellectual History: A Very Short Introduction (2020). Her accomplishments include receiving the Morris D Forkosch Prize for outstanding first book in intellectual history. Beyond academic publications, her essays appear in prominent outlets including The New York Times, The Washington Post, Time, The Guardian, American Scholar, Dissent, and Aeon.
roundtables: Where Have All the Isms Gone?: On the Evolution of Knowledge

name: Mary Ann Caws
achievement: Distinguished Professor, CUNY · 50+ books on modern art and poetry
roundtables: French Surrealism: A Revolution of the Mind

name: Garry Hagberg
roundtables: The Beauty and Unity of Mathematics

name: Lewis Porter
title: Professor of Music
bio: Lewis Porter is long known as a jazz educator and author of books, including the most celebrated volume on John Coltrane, and remains very active as a jazz pianist, keyboardist, and composer. He is known for approaching diverse musical situations with an open attitude. Internationally, he has performed with accomplished musicians including Dave Liebman, Ravi Coltrane, Judi Silvano with Joe Lovano, Jeff Coffin, Jane Ira Bloom, Wycliffe Gordon, Joe Morris, Marc Ribot, George Garzone, Mark Dresser, Gerry Hemingway, Alan Dawson, and Gregg Bendian. He serves as a regular member of Dharma Jazz, an Indian-influenced quartet featuring Badal Roy. A saxophone concerto he composed received premiere performance by Dave Liebman in fall 2012. He has released three albums as leader on the Altrisuoni label and appears on additional collaborative recordings. Critical reception includes characterizations as "a helluva piano player," offering music "founded upon depth and cunning use of space," and being described as "a deep thinker." Porter received a liner-note Grammy nomination in 1996.

name: Nicholas Economides
roundtables: People & Things in Motion: Economics and the Future

name: Timothy O'Connor
title: Professor of Philosophy
bio: O'Connor specializes in metaphysics, philosophy of mind, and philosophy of religion. He earned his doctorate from Cornell University and has held research fellowships at Notre Dame, St. Andrews, and Oxford. He has "delivered 150 academic lectures in 20 countries" and published over 70 scholarly articles. His authored works include Persons and Causes: The Metaphysics of Free Will (2000) and Theism and Ultimate Explanation: The Necessary Shape of Contingency (2008). He is currently working on Thinking About Faith: Philosophy, Science, and Christian Belief. O'Connor has edited or co-edited six volumes, including Religious Faith and Intellectual Virtue (2014), and participates in the Emergence Project at Durham University.

name: Farzad Mahootian
roundtables: Where Have All the Isms Gone?: On the Evolution of Knowledge
Synchronicity: On the Spectrum of Mind and Matter
Synchronicity and Other Mind Matter Conjectures

name: Christopher Wood
title: Carnegie Professor, History of Art; Visiting Professor, Department of German
bio: Wood earned his A.B. from Harvard in 1983 and Ph.D. from Harvard in 1991. He has taught at Yale since 1992 and held visiting positions at UC Berkeley, Vassar College, and Hebrew University in Jerusalem. His fellowships include the Society of Fellows at Harvard, the American Academy in Rome and Berlin, the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton, and the Internationales Forschungszentrum fur Kulturwissenschaften in Vienna. He received the Jacob Wendell Scholarship (1980) and a John Simon Guggenheim Fellowship (2002). From 1999-2002, he served as Book Review Editor of the Art Bulletin. He authored Albrecht Altdorfer and the Origins of Landscape (1993), Forgery, Replica, Fiction: Temporalities of German Renaissance Art (2008, won the Susanne M. Glasscock Humanities Book Prize), and co-authored Anachronic Renaissance (2010). He edited The Vienna School Reader: Politics and Art Historical Method in the 1930s (2000).
roundtables: Aby Warburg: Art, Neuroscience, and Psychoanalysis: Day 1

name: Daphne Merkin
achievement: Author of This Close to Happy · Literary critic

name: Mark Smith
title: Carolina Distinguished Professor of History; Claude Henry Neuffer Chair of Southern Studies; Director of the Institute for Southern Studies
bio: Mark Smith is Carolina Distinguished Professor of History and Claude Henry Neuffer Chair of Southern Studies at the University of South Carolina, where he is also Director of the Institute for Southern Studies. He is a Fellow of the Royal Historical Society. Smith specializes in the history of the senses and is author of a Sensory History Manifesto and editor of Smell and History: A Reader.
roundtables: Discovering the What and the Wherefore: Scents and Sensibility

name: Matthew Stone
title: Associate Professor, Department of Computer Science
bio: Matthew Stone completed his Ph.D. in the Computer and Information Science Department at the University of Pennsylvania in 1998. Since then he has held an appointment in the Computer Science Department and Center for Cognitive Science at Rutgers, the State University of New Jersey. Stone has had visiting positions at the University of Edinburgh and the Universitat Potsdam. His research focuses on problems of meaning in human-human and human-computer conversation.

name: Cristina Alberini
roundtables: Aby Warburg: Art, Neuroscience, and Psychoanalysis: Day 2

name: Carol Rovane
title: Professor of Philosophy
bio: Carol Rovane is Professor of Philosophy at Columbia University, where she has served as Director of Graduate Studies and Chair of the Philosophy Department, and was recently awarded the Lenfest Distinguished Faculty Award. She publishes widely in the areas of metaphysics, philosophy of mind, philosophy of action and ethics, and has authored two books: The Bounds of Agency: An Essay in Revisionary Metaphysics, and The Metaphysics and Ethics of Relativism. Her scholarly work centers on the very idea and nature of a point of view. She examines how different forms of subjectivity -- including bodily perception, phenomenological experience, and rational deliberation -- relate to one another and to objective reality, addressing fundamental questions about mind-world and mind-mind relations.

name: Jonathan Kramnick
roundtables: Coding and the New Human Phenotype: Coding, Fiction, Metafiction -- the Parcellation of What Isn't There
Mind Matters: Past, Present, and Future

name: Frances Pritchett
title: Professor of Modern Indic Languages
bio: Frances Pritchett is Professor of Modern Indic Languages in the Department of Middle Eastern, South Asian, and African Studies at Columbia University. Her research interests include classical Urdu ghazal, especially the work of Ghalib and Mir, and traditional narrative genres in Urdu and Hindi. Pritchett's translation of and commentary on Ghalib's ghazals can be found at her Columbia University website, along with links to her many other contributions to the understanding and appreciation of Urdu and Hindi literatures.
roundtables: Urdu Poetry: Ghalib and the Ghazal

name: Georges Didi-Huberman
roundtables: Aby Warburg: Art, Neuroscience, and Psychoanalysis: Day 1

name: Saeed Tavazoie
title: Professor of Biochemistry, Molecular Biophysics, and Systems Biology
bio: Tavazoie is a systems biologist who was professor in the Department of Molecular Biology and the Institute for Integrative Genomics at Princeton before joining the faculty at Columbia University in 2011. His research focuses on decoding the regulatory genome and revealing how networks of interacting genes implement complex phenotypes, with long-term goals centered on achieving a predictive understanding of biological behavior.
roundtables: Synthetic and Systems Biology: Reinventing the Code of Life

name: Susan Wolfson
title: Professor of English
bio: Wolfson has taught at UC Berkeley and Rutgers University before joining Princeton. She specializes in British Romanticism literature, examining "enlightenment" quests for knowledge and philosophies of social freedom. Her teaching covers Shakespeare, Milton's Paradise Lost, nineteenth-century literature, and Modernism. She developed the Harvard Annotated Edition of Frankenstein (2012) with Ronald Levao and edited the annotated Northanger Abbey (2014). Recent publications include Reading John Keats (Cambridge UP 2015) and Romantic Interactions: Social Being and the Turns of Literary Form (Johns Hopkins UP 2010). She co-edits The Romantics and Their Contemporaries anthology (5th ed. 2012) with Peter Manning.

name: Elias Dakwar
roundtables: Coding and the New Human Phenotype: Is the Universe a Metaverse?

name: Arkady Plotnitsky
title: Distinguished Professor of Literature, Theory and Cultural Studies; Distinguished Professor of Philosophy and Literature
bio: Arkady Plotnitsky is a distinguished professor of Literature, Theory and Cultural Studies Program, and Philosophy and Literature program at Purdue University. He has published nine books, several edited or co-edited collections, and about two hundred articles on continental philosophy, Romantic and modernist literature, the philosophy of mathematics and physics, and the relationships among literature, philosophy, and science. His most recent book is Reality Without Realism: Matter, Thought, and Technology in Quantum Physics (Springer/Nature 2021). His next book Logos and Alogon: The Thinkable and The Unthinkable in Mathematics, from the Pythagoreans to the Moderns is forthcoming from Springer/Nature.

name: Bill Zavatsky
institution: Eugene Lang College of the New School (former); Trinity School in Manhattan (former); Morningside Heights Library (ongoing poetry workshop since 2013)
achievement: Guggenheim Fellow · NEA Fellow · Poet and translator
title: Poet
bio: Bill holds B.A. and M.F.A degrees from Columbia University and has taught across all educational levels since 1971. He authored three poetry collections and completed notable translations, including Andre Breton's Earthlight (with Zack Rogow), which won the PEN/Book-of-the-Month Translation Prize. His work has appeared in major anthologies and recordings by jazz pianists. The New York State Council on the Arts and National Endowment for the Arts both awarded him fellowships. He received MacDowell Colony fellowships in 2007-2008 and a Guggenheim Fellowship in Poetry in 2008.
roundtables: French Surrealism: A Revolution of the Mind

name: Christopher Johnson
roundtables: Aby Warburg: Art, Neuroscience, and Psychoanalysis: Day 2

name: Daphna Shohamy
title: Associate Professor of Psychology
bio: Dr. Shohamy's research combines brain imaging in healthy humans with studies of patients with brain disorders to understand how our expectations and experiences change the way memories are formed and the consequences for health and disease. She is the recipient of Young Investigator Awards from the Cognitive Neuroscience Society, the Society for Neuroeconomics, and the Association for Psychology Science.
roundtables: "Fake" Knowledge: Knowing and the Illusion of Knowing

name: Dennis Yi Tenen
title: Associate Professor, English & Comparative Literature
bio: Tenen is an associate professor at Columbia whose work examines the intersection of people, texts, and technologies. He previously served as a Microsoft engineer and fellow at the Berkman Center for Internet and Society, with code deployed across millions of computers globally. He earned his doctorate in Comparative Literature from Harvard under Elaine Scarry and William Todd's guidance. As co-founder of Columbia's Group for Experimental Methods in Humanistic Research and editor of the On Method series at Columbia University Press, he authored Plain Text: The Poetics of Computation (Stanford University Press, 2017). His scholarship appears in Modern Philology, New Literary History, Amodern, boundary2, and other journals, covering literary theory, media history, and computational narratology. His forthcoming work examines artificial intelligence's creative limitations.
roundtables: Coding and the New Human Phenotype: Are Natural Language Generators for Real?

name: Dorothea von Mücke
title: Professor of Germanic Languages and Literatures
bio: Von Mucke holds a Ph.D. in Comparative Literature from Stanford University and has taught at Columbia since 1988, with visiting professorships in Berlin and Giessen. She specializes in eighteenth-century literature, Romantic literature, and literary theory. Her publications include three books: Virtue and the Veil of Illusion (1991), Body and Text in the Eighteenth Century (1994, co-edited), and The Seduction of the Occult and the Rise of the Fantastic Tale (2003). She co-edited The New History of German Literature (2004) and completed The Practices of the Enlightenment: Aesthetics, Authorship and Audiences, published by Columbia University Press in May 2015.

name: Edwin Turner
title: Professor of Astrophysical Sciences
bio: Turner holds an SB in Physics from MIT (1971) and a PhD in Astronomy from Caltech (1975). He joined Princeton's faculty in 1978 after brief appointments at the Institute for Advanced Study and Harvard. His research spans theoretical and observational astrophysics with over 250 publications covering binary galaxies, dark matter, gravitational lensing, exoplanets, astrobiology, and the origin of life. He directed Apache Point Observatory's 3.5-meter telescope for nine years and served on multiple boards including the Space Telescope Institute Council (three years as Chair). Recent interests include the Breakthrough Starshot Initiative, the YHouse project, artificial intelligence, and consciousness studies.

name: Harry L. Watson
title: Atlanta Distinguished Professor of Southern Culture
bio: Watson is a native of Greensboro, North Carolina, holding a bachelor's degree from Brown University and a doctorate from Northwestern. He joined UNC-CH's History Department in 1976. His scholarly focus encompasses American political history, the early American republic, and the antebellum South. He directed the UNC Center for the Study of the American South (1999-2012) and edited Southern Cultures journal (1993-2019). He has authored or edited eight books, including works on Andrew Jackson versus Henry Clay, Jacksonian politics, and a comprehensive narrative history of the American Republic to 1877.

name: Jared Weinstein
title: Professor, Mathematics & Statistics
bio: Jared Weinstein is a professor in the department of Mathematics and Statistics at Boston University, where he has worked since 2011. He specializes in number theory and its connections to other mathematical fields. A New York native, he earned his PhD from UC Berkeley in 2007.
roundtables: Permanence and Impermanence of Mathematical Concepts

name: Jeremy Veenstra-VanderWeele
title: Mortimer D. Sackler, M.D. Associate Professor of Psychiatry
bio: Dr. Veenstra-VanderWeele is a child and adolescent psychiatrist who uses molecular and translational neuroscience research tools in the pursuit of new treatments for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and related genetic syndromes. His training encompasses human molecular genetics at the University of Chicago and molecular neuroscience at Vanderbilt University. His research focuses on the serotonin, oxytocin and glutamate systems in genetic mouse models with abnormal social or repetitive behavior. He also maintains a clinical/translational program studying novel treatments for autism and Fragile X Syndrome. He joined Columbia University, the New York State Psychiatric Institute, and related affiliated institutions in 2014 to continue developing treatments for children with these conditions.

roundtables: Coding and the New Human Phenotype: Coding, Fiction, Metafiction -- the Parcellation of What Isn't There

roundtables: Synthetic and Systems Biology: Reinventing the Code of Life

name: Polly Young-Eisendrath
institution: Clinical and consulting practice in central Vermont
title: Psychologist, Jungian Psychoanalyst, Mindfulness Teacher, and Speaker
bio: Dr. Young-Eisendrath is a psychologist, speaker, Jungian analyst, and has published 15 books including The Self-Esteem Trap, The Resilient Spirit, Women and Desire, and The Present Heart: A Memoir of Love, Loss and Discovery. She came to psychology and Jungian training through the doorway of Buddhist practice, taking formal Zen vows in 1971. She views the dialogue between Buddhism and psychoanalysis as an emerging healing paradigm where ancient practices of awakening and liberation are meeting up with contemporary models of examining our minds. She is committed to building an interpersonally sustainable and ecologically sane world.

name: Spyros Papapetros
title: Associate Professor of Art and Architectural Theory and Historiography
bio: Spyros Papapetros holds an associate professorship at Princeton, where he also serves on executive committees for European Cultural Studies and Media and Modernity programs, plus holds a Behrman Faculty Fellowship. His scholarly interests encompass intersections among art, architecture, historiography, psychoanalysis, and aesthetics. He has received fellowships from the Getty Research Institute, Institute for Advanced Study, Canadian Center for Architecture, Barr Ferree Foundation, Townsend Center for the Humanities, and the Fulbright Program. During 2002-2003, he was an associate fellow at the Warburg Institute in London, researching unpublished Aby Warburg manuscripts. His published works include On the Animation of the Inorganic: Art, Architecture, and the Extension of Life (University of Chicago Press, 2012) and editorship of Space as Membrane by Siegfried Ebeling (Architectural Association Publications, 2010). His scholarship appears in October, Grey Room, Perspecta, RES, AA Files, Art Bulletin, Oxford Art Journal, and Journal for the Society of Architectural Historians. He co-edited Retracing the Expanded Field (MIT Press, 2014), examining architecture and visual arts intersections. Currently, he is developing World Ornament, examining architectural ornamentation and bodily adornment historiography from mid-19th to mid-20th century.
roundtables: Aby Warburg: Art, Neuroscience, and Psychoanalysis: Day 2

name: Alice Quinn
institution: Poetry Society of America; Columbia University (Adjunct Professor, Graduate School of the Arts)
title: Executive Director, Poetry Society of America
bio: Alice Quinn is the executive director of the Poetry Society of America and an adjunct professor at the Graduate School of the Arts at Columbia University. She was the Poetry Editor of The New Yorker for two decades and before that was an editor at Alfred A. Knopf. Ms. Quinn compiled a collection of Elizabeth Bishop's unpublished work in Edgar Allan Poe & The Juke-Box: Uncollected Poems, Drafts, and Fragments, which appeared in 2006. She is currently preparing a collection of Elizabeth Bishop's journals and notebooks.
roundtables: Elizabeth Bishop: A Conversation about Her Poetry

name: Luis Cabral
roundtables: The Changing Nature of Free Will

name: Miklos Toth
title: Professor of Pharmacology
bio: Toth is a neuroscientist whose laboratory investigates neuropsychiatric disease mechanisms using genetically modified mice to study anxiety, hyperactivity disorders, and behavioral abnormalities. His research examines genetic and environmental risk factors, including early adverse care, sedentary lifestyle, chronic societal stress, psychological trauma, and drug use. The lab explores how environmental stressors can trigger epigenetic changes linked to psychiatric conditions that persist across generations.

name: Rebecca Seal
institution: Departments of Neurobiology and Otolaryngology, Center for Pain Research, University of Pittsburgh
title: Assistant Professor
bio: Dr. Seal is a tenure-track assistant professor in the Departments of Neurobiology and Otolaryngology and the Pittsburgh Center for Pain Research. Her research examines neurotransmitter transporters and their involvement in hearing, vision, motor function, and pain processing. As a postdoctoral scholar at UCSF, she discovered an important role for a specific neurotransmitter transporter in mechanical allodynia. Her laboratory currently investigates neural circuits underlying chronic pain to develop new therapeutic approaches. She has received numerous prestigious awards including recognitions from the Brain and Behavior Research Foundation, Rita Allen Foundation, Hearing Health Foundation, American Diabetes Association, and American Pain Society.

name: Theodore Shapiro
title: Professor Emeritus
bio: Theodore Shapiro is Professor Emeritus at the Weill-Cornell Medical College and a practicing psychoanalyst and adult, child and adolescent psychiatrist. He is a co-principle investigator on a study of psychodynamic psychotherapy for children and adolescents with anxiety disorders. He has more than 200 scholarly and research publications, is author of 7 books, and was Editor of the Journal of the American Psychoanalytic Association from 1983-94. He has received the Rado, Brill, Hartmann, and Philip Wilson Awards and is a training/supervising analyst at New York Psychoanalytic Society and Institute.
roundtables: From Children's Sights to Our Insights: Ethiopian Children's Drawings, Stories and Inner Lives

name: Alma Steingart
title: Assistant Professor, History
bio: Alma Steingart researches the interplay between politics and mathematical rationalities. Her second book manuscript, Accountable Democracy: Mathematical Reasoning and Representative Democracy in America, 1920 to Now, examines how mathematical thought and computing technologies have impacted electoral politics in the United States in the twentieth century. She focuses on the census, apportionment, congressional redistricting, ranked voting, and election forecasts, investigating how changing computational practices have influenced definitions of "fair representation" of the American electorate. In Axiomatics: Mathematical Thought and High Modernism (2023, University of Chicago Press), she excavates the influence of axiomatic reasoning on mid-century American intellectual thought, spanning natural and social sciences, literary criticism, and modern design. Professor Steingart was a Junior Fellow of the Harvard Society of Fellows and a predoctoral research fellow at the Max Planck Institute for the History of Science in Berlin.
roundtables: Permanence and Impermanence of Mathematical Concepts

name: David Rosenthal
title: Professor of Philosophy and Coordinator of the Interdisciplinary Concentration in Cognitive Science
bio: David Rosenthal holds professorships in philosophy at the Graduate Center with courtesy appointments spanning linguistics and cognitive neuroscience. He coordinates the Graduate Center's Interdisciplinary Concentration in Cognitive Science. His scholarly work encompasses consciousness, mental perception, representational thought, emotions, and the self. His 2005 book, Consciousness and Mind, presents his theory that a psychological state is conscious if it is accompanied by a thought to the effect that one is in that state. Additional research addresses emotions, the mind-body problem, and thought-speech relations, with occasional forays into early modern and ancient philosophy plus methodological studies of philosophical history. He previously served as president of the Association for the Scientific Study of Consciousness and held visiting professorships at Nihon University (Tokyo) and Washington University (St. Louis), plus research fellowships at Universities of Bielefeld, Bremen, and Oxford. His credentials include a Ph.D. from Princeton and an A.B. from the University of Chicago.
roundtables: How Deep Do We Go? Behavior, Mind, and The 4-Billion-Year History of Life

name: Aaditya Rangan
title: Associate Professor, Mathematics
bio: Aaditya Rangan is an Associate Professor in the mathematics department at New York University. He received his B.A. from Dartmouth College, his Ph.D. from the University of California at Berkeley, and completed his postdoctoral work at NYU. His research has focused for many years on computational and theoretical models of sensory processing, particularly vision and olfaction.

name: Alan Richardson
achievement: Guggenheim Fellow · NEH Fellow · Philosophy of science
title: Professor of English
bio: Alan Richardson holds degrees in English from Princeton University and Harvard University. Specializing in Romantic literature and culture, he has focused research on gender, childhood and education, race and colonialism, and scientific psychology. Over fifteen years, he has explored connections between literary studies and cognitive sciences. His published works include Literature, Education, and Romanticism: Reading as Social Practice (1994), British Romanticism and the Science of the Mind (2001), and The Neural Sublime: Cognitive Theories and Romantic Texts (2011). He has co-edited special issues and collections addressing Romanticism, slavery, and imperial culture, plus approximately fifty journal articles and book essays. His honors encompass a National Endowment for the Humanities Fellowship, Guggenheim Fellowship, Keats-Shelley Association Distinguished Scholar Award, American Conference on Romanticism book prize, and Alpha Sigma Nu National Jesuit Book Award. Current research examines literary and scientific conceptions of imagination from the Romantic era to the present.

roundtables: Touch as the Ur-Sense: From Presence to Poesy

roundtables: Discovering the What and the Wherefore: Scents and Sensibility

name: Dmitry Rinberg
title: Professor, Department of Neuroscience & Physiology
bio: Dr. Rinberg earned his Ph.D. in Physics from the Weizmann Institute of Science before transitioning to neuroscience research. His work focuses on three main areas: deciphering the fundamental principles of neural coding, exploring olfactory information processing in the brain, and harnessing the olfactory system's remarkable sensitivity as a chemical detector. The lab has developed theoretical frameworks and technologies for brain communication. Beyond his academic role, he directs an NIH-funded consortium called "Cracking the Olfactory Code" involving seven research institutions, and founded Canaery, a startup developing odor digitization through Brain-Machine Interface technology.
roundtables: Discovering the What and the Wherefore: Scents and Sensibility

name: Erica Robles-Anderson
title: Associate Professor of Media, Culture, & Communication
bio: Robles-Anderson holds an Associate Professor position at NYU and received the 2023-24 Leonore Annenberg and Wallis Annenberg Fellowship at Stanford. She serves as editor-in-chief of Public Culture. Her research examines how media technologies create space, particularly configurations that produce public or collective experiences through visibility structures. With training in experimental psychology and cultural history, she employs diverse methodologies to study media-space. Currently, she is authoring a book on 20th-century Protestant worship transformation into mediated "mega-churches" (Yale University Press contract). Previously, she was a Research Fellow in New Media and Architecture at the University of Umea's Department of Culture and Media and Humanities and Technology Laboratory. She holds a Ph.D. in Communication from Stanford University.

roundtables: Panacea or Poison: Placebos and Nocebos in Modern Medicine

name: Paul Zelinsky
institution: Board of the Society of Children's Book Writers and Illustrators; Co-chair of the Children's and Young Adult Committee of PEN American Center
title: Children's Book Illustrator and Author
bio: Paul O. Zelinsky is a children's book illustrator and writer whose books have won wide acclaim and many awards, including the Caldecott Medal for his retelling of Rapunzel, and three Caldecott Honors. He earned an M.F.A. in Painting from Tyler School of Art and a B.A. from Yale College, where he studied under Maurice Sendak. His work spans multiple styles and genres, from Renaissance-inspired oil paintings in fairy tales to cartoonish illustrations. His books communicate effectively with children across developmental levels, including those with learning disabilities or autism. He volunteers with organizations promoting children's literature and literacy.

name: Bonnie Costello
roundtables: Elizabeth Bishop: A Conversation about Her Poetry

name: Dennis Overbye
achievement: Pulitzer Prize finalist (2014) · NY Times Cosmic Affairs Correspondent
title: Cosmic Affairs Correspondent
bio: Dennis Overbye covers science topics ranging from "the mating habits of black holes and zero-gravity fashion shows to science in the movies, the status of Pluto and the fate of the universe" for the New York Times. He authored two books: Lonely Hearts of the Cosmos (1991), a National Book Critics Circle award finalist, and Einstein in Love (2000). His Higgs boson reporting was a Pulitzer Prize finalist in 2014. He has received recognition from the National Academy of Sciences, AAAS, the American Institute for Physics, and the American Astronomical Society. Born in Seattle in 1944, Overbye earned a physics degree from MIT in 1966. He worked at Sky and Telescope and Discover magazines before joining the New York Times in 1998. He resides in New York City with his wife Nancy Wartik and daughter Mira.

name: Elizabeth Waters
title: Democracy and Knowledge Consultant
bio: Elizabeth Waters (Ph.D.) is a democracy and knowledge consultant. Her training in learning and memory neuroscience naturally led her to become an educator. Elizabeth works with students, teachers, and communities to explore the boundaries of our current knowledge and the practices that support this exploration.

name: Jill Gordon
roundtables: Striking a Chord: Hearing and Space

name: Katalin Balog
roundtables: Come Out Wherever You Are: In Search of Consciousness

name: Sandra Shapshay
title: Associate Professor of Philosophy
bio: Shapshay earned her B.A. in Intellectual History from the University of Pennsylvania (1992) and her Ph.D. in Philosophy from Columbia University (2001). Her scholarly interests focus on 19th century German philosophy, especially Kant and Schopenhauer, as well as contemporary aesthetics and ethics. She has published extensively on Schopenhauer's theories of sublime experience and tragedy, including work on environmental aesthetics. Currently, she is developing a book titled Degrees of Inherent Value: Schopenhauer's Ethical Thought, which presents a hybrid Kantian-Moral Sense theory of ethics that promises to interject a novel, less-anthropocentric option into the ethical-theoretical landscape. She has received fellowships from the Deutscher Akademischer Austauschdienst (DAAD) and won the John Eliot Outstanding Teacher Award and a Trustees Teaching Award.

name: Christine Vitrano
title: Associate Professor of Philosophy
bio: Christine Vitrano is the author of The Nature and Value of Happiness. She co-authored Happiness and Goodness: Philosophical Reflections on Living Well with Steven M. Cahn and co-edited Happiness: Classic and Contemporary Readings in Philosophy with him as well.

name: Daniel Goroff
roundtables: The Library as Reality and Metaphor

name: E. James Lieberman
roundtables: Male-Male Competition: Globalization, War, and Violence

name: Ernesto Reuben
title: Assistant Professor of Management
bio: Ernesto Reuben is an Assistant Professor at Columbia Business School whose research focuses on behavioral and public economics. His work examines the role played by social norms and particular psychological traits on activities that are economically relevant for public policy and business strategy. His primary interests include prosocial and antisocial behavior microfoundations, group heterogeneity effects on norm enforcement, and competition's role in team performance. Recent work addresses reciprocity between interest groups and politicians, present-biased preferences and procrastination, and how implicit associations influence expectations and discrimination. He has taught public economics, microeconomics, experimental economics, statistics, and strategy at Princeton University, University of Amsterdam, Norwegian School of Management, and Kellogg School of Management.

name: John McGann
roundtables: Discovering the What and the Wherefore: Scents and Sensibility

name: Karen B. Stern
title: Professor of History
bio: Karen B. Stern is Professor of History at Brooklyn College of the City University of New York. Her research is deeply interdisciplinary. She studied Classics with honors at Dartmouth College, earned her M.A. and Ph.D. in Religious Studies from Brown University, and has excavated and conducted field research in different areas of the Mediterranean, including Jordan, Greece, Tunisia, Morocco, and Israel. Several grants, fellowships, and residencies from the National Endowment for the Humanities, Council of American Overseas Research Centers and the Getty Villa have supported her research, which deploys methods from fields of archaeology, anthropology, epigraphy, history, and religion to investigate the daily lives and material culture of Jews and Christians in antiquity. She is author of Inscribing Devotion and Death: Archaeological Evidence for Jewish Populations of North Africa (Brill 2007); and Writing on the Wall: Graffiti and the Forgotten Jews of Antiquity (2018; paperback ed. 2020), winner of a 2020 Jordan Schnitzer Book Award through the Association for Jewish Studies. She is preparing a museum exhibition on holy graffiti.
roundtables: Coding and the New Phenotype: In Search for Lost Time

name: Michael Novacek
achievement: AAAS Fellow · American Academy of Arts and Sciences · AMNH Senior VP
title: Curator & Professor of Paleontology; Senior Advisor to the Museum's President
bio: Dr. Novacek earned his doctorate from UC Berkeley and specializes in evolutionary patterns and organism relationships across fossil records and DNA sequences. He has led paleontological expeditions across multiple continents including the Rocky Mountains, Andes, Saharan Africa, and Gobi Desert. He authored over 200 publications in peer-reviewed journals and popular media outlets. His notable books include Dinosaurs of the Flaming Cliffs (1996), Time Traveler (2002) -- both New York Times Notable Books -- and Terra: Our 100-Million-Year-Old Ecosystem (2007). He holds fellowships in the American Association for the Advancement of Science and American Academy of Arts and Sciences, plus honors including the 2003 Roy Chapman Andrews Distinguished Explorer's Award and 2005 Lowell Thomas Award.
roundtables: Coding and the New Phenotype: In Search for Lost Time

name: Takis Pappas
title: Author & Researcher
bio: Takis S Pappas holds a PhD from Yale and is a Greek author and researcher currently affiliated with the University of Helsinki. He formerly served as a comparative politics professor at the University of Thessaloniki and has held academic positions at multiple institutions including Strasbourg, Oslo, Freiburg, Luxembourg, Central European University in Budapest, European University Institute in Florence, Yale, and Princeton. His published works include Making Party Democracy in Greece (Macmillan 1999), The Charismatic Party: PASOK, Papandreou, Power (2009), Populism and Crisis Politics in Greece (Palgrave 2014), On the Tightrope: National Crises and Brinkmanship in Greece (2017), Populism and Liberal Democracy: A Comparative and Theoretical Analysis (Oxford University Press 2019), and co-edited European Populism in the Shadow of the Great Recession (ECPR Press 2015). He is currently developing a book examining challengers of European liberal democracy, contributes as a columnist to Kathimerini newspaper, serves as a TED-Ed educator on populism, and maintains a blog on populism and democracy. He divides his time between Brussels and Athens.

name: Mark Polizzotti
achievement: Guggenheim Fellow · Director of Publications, Met Museum
title: Author & Translator; Director of the Publications Program, The Metropolitan Museum of Art
bio: Mark Polizzotti's books include Revolution of the Mind: The Life of Andre Breton, Highway 61 Revisited, Sympathy for the Traitor: A Translation Manifesto, Why Surrealism Matters, and Jump Cuts: Essays on Surrealism, Film, Music, Culture, and Other Utopian Topics. His writings have appeared in Apollo, Bookforum, The Brooklyn Rail, The Nation, The New Republic, The New York Times, The Paris Review, The Wall Street Journal, and elsewhere. His translations of works by Andre Breton, Marguerite Duras, Gustave Flaubert, Patrick Modiano, Scholastique Mukasonga, and Arthur Rimbaud, among others, have won or been shortlisted for the National Book Award, the Oxford-Weidenfeld Translation Prize, the Scott Moncrieff Prize, the International Booker Prize, the English PEN Award, the NBCC/Gregg Barrios Prize, and the French-American Foundation Translation Prize. A member of the American Academy of Arts & Sciences, a Chevalier of the Ordre des Arts et des Lettres, and the recipient of an American Academy of Arts and Letters Award for Literature, he lives in New York, where he directs the publications program at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
roundtables: French Surrealism: A Revolution of the Mind

name: Yi-Yuan Tang
title: Professor of Psychological Sciences, Presidential Endowed Chair in Neuroscience; Founding Director of Texas Tech Neuroimaging Institute
bio: Dr. Tang holds prestigious fellowships with the Association for Psychological Sciences and American Psychological Association. His research spans cognitive, social, and affective neuroscience, examining brain mechanisms underlying attention, mathematics, language, decision-making, and creativity. He developed Integrative Body-Mind Training (IBMT), a mindfulness-based intervention studied since the 1990s through randomized clinical trials. Research demonstrates IBMT reduces stress, enhances attention and cognitive performance, improves emotion regulation and immune function, and promotes neuroplasticity across the lifespan. Applications include addiction, mood disorders, ADHD, mild cognitive impairment, and traumatic brain injury. He has authored 6 books and over 280 peer-reviewed articles published in prestigious venues including Nature, Science, and PNAS, with findings covered by TIME, New York Times, BBC, and NPR.

name: Avner Ash
roundtables: The Beauty and Unity of Mathematics

name: Christopher Mason
roundtables: Synthetic and Systems Biology: Reinventing the Code of Life

name: Craig Newschaffer
title: Professor of Epidemiology and Biostatistics; Founding Director, A.J. Drexel Autism Institute; Associate Dean for Research
bio: Newschaffer serves as founding director of the A.J. Drexel Autism Institute and holds the position of Associate Dean for Research at Drexel's School of Public Health. He is Vice President of the International Society for Autism Research. His research centers on "the discovery of modifiable autism risk factors." He has directed NIH Autism Centers of Excellence projects and led initiatives for ASD case confirmation in epidemiologic research. He holds fellowships and editorial positions with major professional organizations including the American College of Epidemiology.

name: David W. Schwartzman
title: Professor Emeritus, Biology
bio: David W. Schwartzman holds a PhD in Geochemistry from Brown University. He published "Life, Temperature and the Earth" through Columbia University in 1999, updated in paperback in 2002, alongside numerous contributions to "Capitalism Nature Socialism" and other academic journals. His recent works include "The Earth is Not for Sale" (2019), co-authored with his son Peter, and "The Global Solar Commons" (2021). He serves on advisory boards for "Capitalism Nature Socialism" and the editorial board of "Science & Society." His activism includes membership in the DC Statehood Green Party and the Green Party of the United States, where he participates in International and EcoAction Committees.
roundtables: People & Things in Motion: Economics and the Future

name: Eric Steinhart
title: Professor of Philosophy
bio: Eric Steinhart grew up on a farm in Pennsylvania. He received his BS in Computer Science from the Pennsylvania State University, after which he worked as a software designer for several years. Many of his algorithms have been patented. He earned an MA in Philosophy from Boston College and was awarded a PhD in Philosophy from SUNY at Stony Brook. He has taught in the Philosophy Departments at Dartmouth College and William Paterson University. His books have concerned Nietzsche, the logic of metaphor, mathematics, and life after death. Much of his work involves the application of new computational concepts to solve old philosophical problems. He loves New England and the American West, and enjoys all types of hiking and biking, chess, microscopy, and photography.

name: Gail Weiss
title: Professor of Philosophy
bio: Weiss has recently served as Executive Co-Director of the Society for Phenomenology and Existentialism (SPEP) and as General Secretary for the International Merleau-Ponty Circle. Her scholarly work spans phenomenology, feminist theory, critical race theory, disability studies, literature, and queer theory. She has authored monographs including Refiguring the Ordinary (2008) and Body Images: Embodiment as Intercorporeality (1999), and co-edited 50 Concepts for a Critical Phenomenology (2020). Her research examines how sexist, racist, ageist and ableist understandings of "normal bodies" shape lived experience.

name: George Reeke, Jr.
title: Associate Professor & Head, Laboratory of Biological Modeling
bio: George Reeke holds tenure as Associate Professor and directs the Laboratory of Biological Modeling at The Rockefeller University, serving also as a Senior Fellow of The Neurosciences Institute. His educational background includes a B.S. from Caltech (Baxter Prize recipient), plus M.A. and Ph.D. degrees from Harvard University. He received both a National Science Foundation Predoctoral Fellowship and an Alfred P. Sloan Research Fellowship. His early career involved protein crystallography training under Dick Marsh at Caltech and Bill Lipscomb at Harvard. His doctoral research produced one of the first atomic coordinate sets for any protein, that of the enzyme carboxypeptidase A. At Rockefeller University since 1970, he collaborated with Gerald Edelman on protein structures relevant to immune system function. He developed early microprocessor-controlled laboratory instruments and X-ray camera technology. From the late 1970s onward, his research shifted toward pattern recognition, perceptual categorization, and motor control through neuronal system simulations. Notable collaborative projects include brain-based robot networks with Edelman's group, computational neuron modeling methods with Allan Coop, neuronal spike train analysis techniques, primate visual cortex models with Valentin Piech, bird song learning models with Cameron Wellock, and anesthetic propofol mechanism studies with Kingsley Storer. Additionally, he directs the Peggy Rockefeller Concerts, serves on the Journal of Integrative Neuroscience editorial board, and has authored approximately 100 scientific papers.
roundtables: What Can Mathematics Teach Us About Mind/Brain?

name: Hava Tirosh-Samuelson
title: Regents' Professor, Irving and Miriam Lowe Professor of Modern Judaism, Director of Jewish Studies, and Professor of History
bio: Professor Tirosh-Samuelson earned her Ph.D. from Hebrew University in 1978. Her scholarly focus centers on Jewish intellectual history, religion and science, and religious environmentalism. She has authored two award-winning books: Between Worlds: The Life and Work of Rabbi David ben Judah Messer Leon (1991) and Happiness in Premodern Judaism: Virtue, Knowledge and Well-Being in Premodern Judaism (2003). She edited eight volumes including works on Hans Jonas, transhumanism, and human futures. She served as editor-in-chief for a 20-book series on contemporary Jewish philosophers. Her research on religion, science, and technology has been supported by three major grants between 2006-2018, funding symposia, lectures, seminars, and conferences. She participates in the International Society of Science and Religion, serves on Zygon: Journal of Religion and Science's editorial board, and manages the Judaism, Science and Medicine Group.

name: Louis Rose
title: Professor of Modern European History; Editor of American Imago
bio: Louis Rose is Professor of Modern European History at Otterbein University in Ohio, a member of the Trustees of the Sigmund Freud Archives, Library of Congress, and the Editor of American Imago. His scholarly work includes The Freudian Calling: Early Viennese Psychoanalysis and the Pursuit of Cultural Science (Wayne State University, 1998), which won the 1999 Austrian Cultural Institute Prize for Best Book in Austrian Studies, and The Survival of Images: Art Historians, Psychoanalysts, and the Ancients (Wayne State University, 2001). He holds a B.A. in History from Clark University and a Ph.D. in History from Princeton University, and was a Fulbright Fellow in Vienna. He served as editor for the Fall 2013 issue of American Imago, focused on psychoanalysis, neuroscience, and European modernism.
roundtables: Aby Warburg: Art, Neuroscience, and Psychoanalysis: Day 2

name: Michelle Woods
title: Associate Professor of English
bio: Michelle Woods specializes in translation studies and literature. She authored three books: Kafka Translated (Bloomsbury, 2013), Censoring Translation (Continuum, 2012), and Translating Milan Kundera (Multilingual Matters, 2006). Currently editing Authorizing Translation (Routledge, 2016) and serves as co-editor of Bloomsbury's Literatures, Cultures, Translation series. Her background includes Irish and Czech heritage, with published translations in Granta and Words Without Borders. She holds degrees from Trinity College Dublin and fellowships from Fulbright (Columbia) and IRCHSS (Dublin City University).

name: Morris Vogel
title: President, the Tenement Museum
bio: Vogel trained as an American social and urban historian at Brandeis University (B.A. 1967) and the University of Chicago (Ph.D. 1974). He joined Temple University's faculty in Philadelphia in 1973, becoming a professor in 1985 and serving as dean of the College of Liberal Arts from 1999-2003. He subsequently directed the Rockefeller Foundation's Creativity and Culture Program. Vogel authored or edited six books on American social and cultural history, including The Invention of the Modern Hospital and Cultural Connections. He co-founded and directed an NEH-funded regional humanities center and served on Pennsylvania's Historic Preservation Board. Vogel was born in Kazakhstan to stateless refugee parents. He resides in Manhattan with his wife Ruth, a clinical psychologist, and has two adult sons.

name: Pascal Massie
roundtables: Touch as the Ur-Sense: From Presence to Poesy

name: Sean Singer
institution: Rutgers-Newark (teaches English and African American Studies)
title: Poet
bio: Sean Singer's first book, Discography, won the Yale Series of Younger Poets Prize, selected by W.S. Merwin, and the Norma Farber First Book Award from the Poetry Society of America. He has also published two chapbooks, Passport and Keep Right On Playing Through the Mirror Over the Water, both with Beard of Bees Press, and is the recipient of a Fellowship from the National Endowment for the Arts. His poetry, reviews, creative nonfiction, and essays have recently appeared in Memorious, Pleiades, Sou'wester, Iowa Review, New England Review, and Salmagundi. He is writing his dissertation in American Studies at Rutgers-Newark, where he teaches English and African American Studies. He lives in New York City.

name: Stephen Ross
title: Research Associate Professor, Psychiatry and Child & Adolescent Psychiatry
bio: Dr. Ross is a founding member of the NYU Psychedelic Research Group and associate director of the Center for Psychedelic Medicine at NYU Langone Health, where he also directs the Psychedelic Medicine Research Training Program. Over 21 years at NYU and Bellevue, he has held multiple leadership positions including Director of the Division of Alcoholism and Drug Abuse (12 years), Director of Addiction Psychiatry, and Director of the Addiction Psychiatry Fellowship. His research focuses on developing novel pharmacologic-psychosocial approaches to treating addiction, cancer-related distress, depression, PTSD, and personality disorders. He leads several psychedelic-focused clinical trials including psilocybin-assisted psychotherapy for cancer patients, LSD-assisted therapy for cancer pain, psilocybin treatment for alcohol use disorder and major depression, and MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for PTSD. He also studies cannabinoid therapeutics.

name: Tapomayukh Bhattacharjee
roundtables: Touch as the Ur-Sense: From Presence to Poesy

name: Andrea Pinotti
title: Professor of Aesthetics, Department of Philosophy
bio: Andrea Pinotti teaches Aesthetics at the Universita degli Studi di Milano and serves as Directeur de Programme at the College International de Philosophie in Paris on the project Monument Nonument. His research focuses on Kunstwissenschaft (Riegl, Wolfflin, Warburg), image-theories, and empathy-theories. He held fellowships at Columbia University's Italian Academy for Advanced Studies, was Directeur d'etudes associe at EHESS in Paris, Senior Fritz Saxl-Fellow at the Warburg Institute in London, and Gastwissenschaftler at the ZfL in Berlin. Pinotti has edited Italian texts by empathy and art theorists including Robert Vischer, Friedrich Theodor Vischer, Theodor Lipps, Moritz Geiger, Alois Riegl, Heinrich Wolfflin, Wilhelm Worringer, and Hans Sedlmayr. His major publications include The Body of Style (1998), Memories of the Neutral (2001), and Empathy: History of an Idea from Plato to the Post-Human (2011). He co-edited Images of the Mind (2007), Image-Theories (2009), and Art History and Visual Studies in Europe (2012).
roundtables: Aby Warburg: Art, Neuroscience, and Psychoanalysis: Day 1

name: Anna Shechtman
achievement: Author of The Riddles of the Sphinx · Yale professor
title: Klarman Fellow; Assistant Professor in the Department of Literatures in English (beginning 2024)
bio: Anna Shechtman is a Klarman Fellow at Cornell University and will begin as an assistant professor in the Department of Literatures in English in 2024. She is writing a two-volume history of the 'media' and 'data' concepts in the United States. The first book builds upon her dissertation, The Media Concept: A Genealogy, which demonstrates that the imperial spread of the media concept has imperiled the very values it was initially employed to defend. The second, Data: A Humanistic Inquiry, challenges the notion that 'data' has always been the proprietary domain of social scientists, improperly imported into the study of literature and history by so-called digital humanists. Her first book The Riddles of the Sphinx, about the history of the crossword puzzle and the sexual politics of wordplay, will be published by HarperOne in March. Her freelance essays and reviews have appeared in ArtForum, The New Inquiry, The New Yorker, The New York Review of Books, Slate, The Yale Review, and the Los Angeles Review of Books, where she is an editor-at-large.

name: Clare Batty
roundtables: Discovering the What and the Wherefore: Scents and Sensibility

name: Ellen Handler Spitz
title: Honors College Professor of Visual Arts
bio: Ellen Handler Spitz writes, teaches, and lectures on the visual, literary, and performing arts and psychology and on the aesthetic lives of children. Her background encompasses four years as a research candidate at Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research, plus the 2008 Erikson Scholar position at Austen Riggs. She has held residential fellowships at the Getty Center, Bunting Institute at Harvard, Clark Art Institute, Stanford's Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences, Camargo Foundation in France, and Rutgers Center for Children and Childhood Studies. She is a fellow of the New York Institute for the Humanities. She authored numerous works including Art and Psyche, Image and Insight, Museums of the Mind, Inside Picture Books, The Brightening Glance, Illuminating Childhood, and Freud and Forbidden Knowledge (co-edited). Her reviews appeared in The New York Times, The New Republic, and she contributes to Artcritical. Her work has been translated into Italian, Japanese, and Serbian, with recent research focusing on art illustration and children's aesthetic development.
roundtables: From Children's Sights to Our Insights: Ethiopian Children's Drawings, Stories and Inner Lives

name: Francis X. Shen
title: Executive Director, Harvard MGH Center for Law, Brain, and Behavior
bio: Dr. Shen is the Executive Director of the Harvard MGH Center for Law, Brain, and Behavior and an Instructor in Psychology at Harvard Medical School. He holds positions as Senior Fellow in Law and Applied Neuroscience at Harvard Law School's Petrie-Flom Center and as Associate Professor of Law and McKnight Presidential Fellow at the University of Minnesota, where he directs the Shen Neurolaw Lab. He serves as Executive Director of Education and Outreach for the MacArthur Foundation Research Network on Law and Neuroscience. Born and raised in St. Louis, Missouri, he earned his B.A. from the University of Chicago, J.D. from Harvard Law School, and Ph.D. from Harvard University. His research focuses on law and neuroscience intersections, including memory, lie detection, cognitive enhancement, criminal justice, brain injury, sports concussion, and artificial intelligence law. He has co-authored three books, including the first Law and Neuroscience casebook.

name: Greg Calbi
roundtables: Music to Whose Ears? Music, Emotion, and Mind

name: Ilya Tëmkin
title: Professor of Biology; Research Associate at the National Museum of Natural History (Smithsonian Institution)
bio: An interdisciplinary scientist examining how evolution works in nature and in human culture in the general framework of the hierarchy theory. He specializes in bivalve mollusks and analyzes ecological, historical, and developmental factors in diversification. His cultural research explores musical instrument design as a model for understanding information transmission mechanisms. He coedited Evolutionary Theory: A Hierarchical Perspective (Chicago University Press, 2016). Academic background includes a doctorate in Biology from NYU and bachelor's degree from Columbia University, with postdoctoral fellowships at the American Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution, and Museum National d'Histoire Naturelle in Paris.

name: Joanne Ruthsatz
title: Assistant Professor of Psychology
bio: Joanne Ruthsatz is Assistant Professor of Psychology at The Ohio State University, Mansfield. She graduated from Bowling Green State University with a BA in psychology, receiving Phi Beta Kappa. She completed her PhD in Experimental Psychology at Case Western Reserve University. Training on the Mental Retardation Research Grant, she studied the full range of human cognitive ability. Her research interests include discovering the genetic link between autism and the extraordinary talent displayed by child prodigies. Her forthcoming book is titled The Prodigy's Cousin: The Family Link Between Autism and Extraordinary Talent.

name: Joe Peyronnin
title: Professor of Journalism at NYU; Former Associate Professor of Journalism at Hofstra University
bio: Peyronnin has been an adjunct journalism professor at NYU since 2008 and served as a full-time associate professor at Hofstra University from 2011-2019, earning "Teacher of the Year" in 2017. He spent 40 years as an award-winning broadcast journalism executive at CBS News, Fox News, and Telemundo/NBC News. At Telemundo (1999-2006), he created the network's first news division as Executive Vice President. The organization won an Emmy for its 9/11 coverage and received critical acclaim for Iraq War reporting. He served as Fox News President (1995-1996), establishing foundational structures for the network and creating "Fox News Sunday." From 1989-1996, he was Vice President and Assistant to the President for CBS News, overseeing major programs including "60 Minutes," "48 Hours," and "The CBS Evening News." Earlier roles included CBS News Washington Bureau Chief (1987-1989) and senior producer for "CBS Evening News with Dan Rather" (1982-1987), where he covered White House, Congress, U.S.-Soviet summits, and met presidents from Nixon to George W. Bush. He holds Emmy Awards for breaking news and a Polk Award for Tiananmen Square coverage. Board memberships include Vibrant Emotional Health and Gracie Square Hospital. He earned a BA in Broadcasting from Columbia College Chicago (1970) and an MBA from Roosevelt University (1978).

name: Jonathan Stray
title: Research Scholar; Computational Journalist
bio: Jonathan Stray is a computational journalist at Columbia University, where he teaches the dual masters degree in computer science and journalism and leads the development of Workbench, an integrated tool for data journalism. He has contributed to The New York Times, The Atlantic, Wired, Foreign Policy and ProPublica. He was formerly the Interactive Technology Editor at the Associated Press, a freelance reporter in Hong Kong, and a graphics algorithm designer for Adobe Systems.

name: Maria G. Pisano
title: Book Artist, Printmaker, Curator & Educator
bio: Maria G. Pisano is a book artist, printmaker, curator and educator who publishes work under the Memory Press imprint. Her pieces are held in prestigious collections including The Library of Congress, 9-11 Memorial Museum, National Library of Medicine, Columbia University, New York Public Library, and Stanford University. Her book Caudex Folium appears in the "Towers Rising" exhibit at the 9-11 Memorial Museum in NYC. In 2022, her work was featured in "And Yet We Rise: A Retrospect of the Days and Times Surrounding 9/11" at the American Consulate in London. She has curated multiple exhibitions, including Book as Witness: The Artist's Response at Center for Book Arts and Crossroads: Book Artists' Impassioned Responses to Immigration, Human Rights and Our Environment at the Hunterdon Museum of Art. She contributes to book arts publications, lectures at major institutions, and conducts workshops nationally and internationally.

name: Maura Spiegal
title: Co-Director, Division of Narrative Medicine; Senior Lecturer, Department of English & Comparative Literature
bio: Professor Maura Spiegel holds dual leadership roles in narrative medicine and English studies at Columbia. Her teaching emphasizes fiction and film with thematic focus on family, memory, place, and affect. She previously served seven years as co-editor-in-chief of Literature and Medicine (Hopkins U.P.). Her publications include co-authorship of The Grim Reader: Writings on Death, Dying and Living On (Anchor/Doubleday) and The Principles and Practice of Narrative Medicine (Oxford University Press), plus a biography of filmmaker Sidney Lumet (St. Martin's Press). She regularly contributes to The New York Times, Newsday, and other publications.

name: Maxine Sheets-Johnstone
title: Courtesy Professor of Philosophy
bio: Maxine Sheets-Johnstone is a philosopher whose first life was as a dancer/choreographer and dance professor/scholar. She maintains an ongoing Courtesy Professor appointment in the Department of Philosophy at the University of Oregon where she taught periodically in the 1990s. She has published numerous articles in humanities, art, and science journals, with recent publications in Psychotherapy and Politics International and Anthropological Theory. Her authored books include The Phenomenology of Dance; The Roots of Thinking; The Roots of Power: Animate Form and Gendered Bodies; The Roots of Morality; The Primacy of Movement; and The Corporeal Turn: An Interdisciplinary Reader. She earned an M.A. in Dance and a Ph.D. in Dance and Philosophy from the University of Wisconsin, where she also pursued but did not complete a second doctorate in evolutionary biology. She received a Distinguished Fellowship from the Institute of Advanced Study at Durham University, UK, for her xenophobia research during its inaugural year, themed "The Legacy of Charles Darwin."
roundtables: Male-Male Competition: Globalization, War, and Violence

name: Adam J. Sacks
title: Ph.D. Candidate in History
bio: Adam J Sacks is pursuing doctoral studies in history at Brown University. He earned a Master of Arts from Brown University, a Master of Science with High Honors from City College of CUNY, and a Bachelor of Arts Summa Cum Laude with Phi Beta Kappa honors from Cornell University. His fellowship experience includes serving as an "Auschwitz Jewish Center Fellow under the auspices of the Museum of Jewish Heritage in New York" in 2010, and holding the Cahnmann Foundation Fellowship at the Center for Jewish History in 2011-2012. He received the Dissertation Grant from the Central European History Society and served as a Leo Baeck Programme fellow in 2012-2013 at Berlin's Universitat der Kunste. Currently, he holds a Doctoral Fellowship in Advanced Shoah Studies with the Claims Conference for Jewish Material Claims Against Germany. His scholarly interests focus on cultural responses to catastrophe, trauma, war, genocide, and cultural representation. His work has appeared in New German Critique, the Association for Jewish Studies Journal, and forthcoming conference proceedings.
roundtables: Trauma and its Aftereffects, Part I: War and Genocide

name: Dan Slater
institution: Freelance (contributor to Fast Company, The New York Times, The Washington Post, New York Magazine, GQ)
title: Journalist, Author
bio: Dan Slater, a widely published author of journalism and creative nonfiction, is the author of Love in the Time of Algorithms: What Technology Does to Meeting and Mating. A former legal affairs reporter for The Wall Street Journal, Dan is currently a contributor to Fast Company and The New York Times. He also writes for The Washington Post, New York Magazine, and GQ. Slater is a graduate of Colgate University and Brooklyn Law School.

name: Jasper St. Bernard
title: Visiting Assistant Professor, History
bio: Jasper St. Bernard is a Visiting Assistant Professor of History at Rhodes College. His academic work currently focuses on African American philosophy, focusing primarily on the late 19th and early 20th centuries. His recently completed dissertation explored the anti-lynching work of Ida B. Wells-Barnett. While his work focuses on the social/political thought of black people during the lynching era, the topics he has written on have varied. In The Routledge Handbook of Philosophy and Implicit Cognition (2022), he co-wrote a chapter with Dr. Shaun Gallagher, "Race and the implicit aspects of embodied social interaction," exploring the role the body and early childhood have in the development of one's implicit biases. He also co-wrote an article with Dr. Verena Erlenbusch-Anderson, "'Just the Same as Fascism for Us': The Black Panther Party's Antifascist Thought and Praxis" (2023). He most recently joined a group of international thinkers in a book project, Ubuntu: Interdisciplinary Conversations Across Continents (2023), contributing a chapter titled "'To Shine the Light of Truth': Ubuntu and the Lynching Era in America."

name: Jessica Tyler
title: Professor, Department of Epigenetics and Molecular Carcinogenesis
bio: Jessica Tyler was born in England in 1969. After graduating from the University of Sheffield with a Bachelors degree and Hans Krebs prize in Biochemistry, she performed her PhD studies at the MRC Virology Unit in Glasgow, Scotland. During postdoctoral work at UC San Diego, she identified factors packaging genetic material into chromosomes. She held a faculty position at the University of Colorado School of Medicine from 2000, where she revealed roles of chromosome structure in aging and other processes. She received the Charlotte Friend Woman in Cancer Research Award (2009) and was a Leukemia and Lymphoma Society Scholar before relocating to MD Anderson in 2010.

name: Patricia Olynyk
title: Artist; former Chair of the Leonardo Education and Art Forum; Co-Director of the NY LASER program
bio: Olynyk's artistic practice explores intersections of art, science, and technology, examining "the dialectics of natural and artificial, and cognition and affect." She appropriates scientific imaging technologies in installations, photographs, and videos to investigate how interpretation shifts between "fact and speculation." Her career includes developing interdisciplinary curricula and programming at research institutions, with particular focus on fostering "third culture" collaborations across creative and scientific domains.

name: Sushma Subramanian
title: Science Writer & Journalist; Associate Professor of Journalism
bio: Subramanian authored "How to Feel: The Science and Meaning of Touch," exploring scientific, physical, emotional, and cultural dimensions of touch to reconnect readers with arguably our most important sense. Her journalism focuses on scientific research affecting daily life experiences, published in outlets including The Atlantic, The New York Times, Scientific American, Discover, and Elle. She teaches journalism at the University of Mary Washington in Virginia. Her fellowships include support from The Pulitzer Center on Crisis Reporting, National Evolutionary Synthesis Center at Duke, Genetics and Behavior Journalism Fellowship at UVA, Center for Health Journalism at USC, Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT, International Women's Media Foundation, and Economic Hardship Reporting Project.
roundtables: Touch as the Ur-Sense: From Presence to Poesy

name: Anne-Marie Levine
roundtables: French Surrealism: A Revolution of the Mind

name: Brigitte Kahl
roundtables: The Changing Nature of Free Will

name: David Russell
title: Associate Professor, English
bio: David Russell is an Associate Professor of English at UCLA who teaches nineteenth-century literature, film, philosophy and psychoanalysis. He authored two books: Marion Milner: On Creativity (Oxford University Press, 2024) and Tact: Aesthetic Liberalism and the Essay Form in Nineteenth-Century Britain (Princeton University Press, 2018).

name: François Quiviger
title: Curator of Digital Resources, Assistant Librarian
bio: Francois Quiviger earned his Ph.D. from the Warburg Institute in London, where he serves as curator of digital resources, librarian, and researcher. His scholarly focus encompasses early modern European academies, mythology, and Renaissance material culture alongside art and art theory. His 2010 publication, "The Sensory World of Italian Renaissance Art" (London, Chicago), examines how sensation functioned in Renaissance thought and practice, exploring connections to mental imagery and Renaissance artists' techniques for making touch, sound, and scent perceptible to audiences' minds.

name: Gilbert Rose
institution: Yale University; Western New England Institute for Psychoanalysis (former faculty)
title: Member of the Muriel Gardiner Program in Psychoanalysis and the Humanities
bio: Gilbert J. Rose served for many years on the faculties of Yale University Medical School and the Western New England Institute for Psychoanalysis. He has received the Sandor Lorand Essay Award and The Founders Teaching Prize. His professional standing includes Distinguished Life Fellow status with the American Psychiatric Association and Life Member status with the American Psychoanalytic Association. He maintains a private psychiatry and psychoanalysis practice in Rowayton, Connecticut. His published works include The Power of Form: A Psychoanalytic Approach to Aesthetic Form, Trauma and Mastery in Life and Art; Necessary Illusion: Art As Witness; and Between Couch and Piano: Psychoanalysis, Music, Art, Neuroscience.
roundtables: Music to Whose Ears? Music, Emotion, and Mind

name: Jesse Harris
roundtables: Music to Whose Ears? Music, Emotion, and Mind

name: John Schaefer
title: Host and producer of WNYC's "New Sounds" and "Soundcheck"; creator of "The Furthermore" on WQXR
bio: Schaefer hosts and produces WNYC's long-running new music program "New Sounds," established in 1982, alongside its "Soundcheck" podcast featuring live performances and interviews since 2002. He launched "The Furthermore" on WQXR in January 2017. He founded the New Sounds Live concert series in 1986, showcasing new works and commissioned pieces, held primarily at Brookfield Place and Merkin Concert Hall in New York. His published works include "New Sounds: A Listener's Guide to New Music" (Harper & Row, 1987; Virgin Books, 1990), contributions to the "Cambridge Companion to Singing: World Music" (Cambridge University Press, 2000), and the television program "Bravo Profile: Bobby McFerrin" (2003). Additionally, he authored "Bloodlines: A Horse Racing Anthology" (Vintage, 2006) and served as a panelist on the BBC's "Sports World."

name: Michael Waldholz
title: Medical Science Writer and Media Consultant
bio: Waldholz recently served six years as managing editor at Bloomberg News/Businessweek, following a 25-year career at the Wall Street Journal in various writing and editorial roles. His Bloomberg responsibilities encompassed health care and science coverage, including pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, insurance, medical services, and health policy. He authored "Curing Cancer" and co-authored "Genome." He received the 1996 Pulitzer Prize for national reporting for AIDS medicine breakthrough stories.
roundtables: Synthetic and Systems Biology: Reinventing the Code of Life

roundtables: Urdu Poetry: Ghalib and the Ghazal

name: Phil Zabriskie
institution: N/A (formerly Editorial Director for Doctors Without Borders USA)
title: Author and Journalist
bio: Zabriskie authored The Kill Switch, a Kindle Single examining how American combat personnel process their experiences taking life in warfare and reintegrating afterward. He spent nearly a decade as an overseas journalist, primarily with Time magazine covering Asia and the Middle East, including Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, Israel, Palestinian Territories, Indonesia, Philippines, and Vietnam. His writing has appeared in National Geographic, New York, Fortune, and the Washington Post Magazine, focusing on people from numerous different societies living with trauma and its aftermath. He held fellowships with the Dart Foundation for Journalism and Trauma, spoke at the State Department and New America Foundation conferences, and received Princeton University's 1994 Bates Farnham Outstanding Achievement Award for making a deep and meaningful contribution to the world.
roundtables: Trauma and its Aftereffects, Part I: War and Genocide

name: Theodore Dimon
roundtables: Human and Nonhuman Minds: Continuities and Discontinuities

name: Wendy Sloan
title: Poet, Translator, Essayist; Retired Attorney
bio: Sloan is a poet, translator, essayist, and retired attorney who previously practiced labor law with her partner. Her poetry has appeared in multiple journals and anthologies including The Able Muse Translation Issue and The Great American Wise Ass Poetry Anthology. She published Sunday Mornings at the Caffe Mediterraneum (Kelsay Books, 2016). Her achievements include finalist status in the Howard Nemerov Sonnet Award Competition, multiple Pushcart Prize nominations, and a Readers' Choice Award from Orbis for her translation of Gaspara Stampa's Sonnet 208. She collaborated with artist Holly Trostle Brigham on Amicizia, an imagined friendship book about Baroque Italian artists Artemisia Gentileschi and Giovanna Garzoni, launched at the Rosenbach Museum and Library in Philadelphia.

name: Wynn Schwartz
institution: The Massachusetts School of Professional Psychology; Harvard Medical School; Harvard Extension School
title: Clinical psychologist and research psychoanalyst
bio: Dr. Schwartz holds core faculty status at The Massachusetts School of Professional Psychology and teaches at Harvard Medical School and Harvard Extension School. He serves as coeditor of "Advances in Descriptive Psychology" and previously taught at Wellesley College, Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute, and Massachusetts Institute of Psychoanalysis. His empirical research examines dreaming, memory, problem representation, hypnosis, and episodic memory. Using Descriptive Psychology, he focuses on theory-free formulations of action and responsibility, hypnosis concepts, psychotherapy status dynamics, and empathic action parameters. Current research explores liberation, improvisation, play, and behavioral logic of social progress. He maintains a Boston-based psychotherapy and supervision practice serving individuals and couples.

name: Nathan M. Szajnberg
institution: San Francisco Center for Psychoanalysis; New York Psychoanalytic Society and Institute (Faculty); formerly Freud Professor of Psychoanalysis at the Hebrew University
title: Wallerstein Research Fellow in Psychoanalysis
bio: Nathan Szajnberg holds the position of Wallerstein Research Fellow in Psychoanalysis at the San Francisco Center for Psychoanalysis and serves on the Faculty at New York Psychoanalytic Society and Institute. He formerly held the Freud Professor of Psychoanalysis position at the Hebrew University. He authored or edited four books and one novella: "Educating the Emotions" (examining Bruno Bettelheim's concepts), "Lives Across Time" (co-authored with Henry Massie), "Reluctant Warriors" (exploring maturation and inner psychological development of elite Israeli military personnel), and "Sheba and Solomon's Return: Ethiopian Children in Israel" (the foundational research for the roundtable). His academic training included studies at University of Chicago College and Medical School under mentors including Bruno Bettelheim and Saul Bellow. He graduated from the St. Louis Psychoanalytic Institute and serves as a Training Analyst for both the Israel Psychoanalytic Society and the International Psychoanalytic Association.
roundtables: From Children's Sights to Our Insights: Ethiopian Children's Drawings, Stories and Inner Lives
